planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained woodland soil in dappled to deep shade; the clump is slow to establish in its first two seasons but then spreads steadily and needs no further attention.

directions: Syneilesis palmata emerges in spring with silvery, deeply cut, umbrella-like leaves that unfurl from a tightly pleated cone before flattening into broad, palmately lobed foliage held on wiry stems. As the season progresses the leaves turn glossy green and the clump sends up airy, fuzzy pink-white flower heads in mid-to-late summer, followed by slow spread via creeping rhizomes into an attractive woodland colony. Plant divisions in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in dappled to deep shade, where this East Asian woodlander is slow to establish but essentially permanent and pest-free once settled. It pairs well with hosta, rodgersia, and ferns as a textural foil in a shaded border.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall into rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and slug pressure while the clump establishes.

directions: Hosta kiyosumiensis is a robust wild species native to moist mountain woodlands on Japan's Boso Peninsula, forming broad mounds of glossy, deeply veined, heart-shaped leaves that are larger and more lustrous than many garden hybrids. In mid-to-late summer it sends up tall scapes of pale lavender, bell-shaped flowers above the foliage, and the species has long been used by breeders for leaf substance and sheen in modern hosta cultivars. Grow it in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Established clumps are long-lived and slowly expand into dense, weed-suppressing colonies.
sources: W. George Schmid, The Genus Hosta

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give this large species ample room, as mature clumps become substantial over two to three seasons.

directions: Hosta fluctuans is one of the largest-leaved wild hosta species, native to Yakushima Island off southern Japan, and is best known as the wild parent behind the popular variegated cultivar 'Sagae.' Its thick, glossy, deeply corrugated leaves ripple and twist along the margin, giving the species its descriptive name, and mature clumps can reach imposing proportions. Pale lavender flowers rise on tall scapes above the foliage in summer. Site it in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in partial to full shade where its bold texture can anchor a woodland or shade border planting.
sources: W. George Schmid, The Genus Hosta

planting.note: Divide and transplant rhizome clumps in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; water well until new growth confirms establishment, then let the rhizomes knit together into a spreading mat.

directions: Ophiopogon bodinieri is a grassy, evergreen, rhizomatous groundcover native to woodland and rocky slopes across much of China, forming dense spreading mats of narrow, arching, dark green leaves that are considerably more cold-hardy than the more commonly grown Ophiopogon japonicus. Pale lilac to white flowers nod along short spikes hidden among the foliage in summer, followed by small blue-black berries in fall. It spreads steadily by underground rhizomes to knit together a durable, low-maintenance groundcover in humus-rich, well-drained soil. Divide and transplant clumps in spring to establish new drifts.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizome divisions 3-4 inches deep in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained woodland soil around the last frost date, in partial to full shade; mulch heavily over winter where marginally hardy.

directions: Cautleya gracilis is a slender, cold-hardier relative of the more commonly grown Cautleya spicata, native to moist Himalayan forest understories from Nepal through southwestern China. Slim reed-like stems carry narrow, lance-shaped leaves and are topped in late summer by short spikes of bright yellow, hooded flowers set against maroon-red bracts, a striking combination for a shaded border. The rhizomatous clump dies back to the ground after frost and resprouts reliably from a deep, mulched planting the following spring. Give it rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from drying wind.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
